summary: Gives recommendations for how a stateless IPv4/IPv6 translator should translate source addresses of ICMPv6 packets when the address cannot be translated to IPv4. Such packets should still be passed across the translator as ICMP packets directed to the IPv4 destination. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A translator turns IPv6 messages into IPv4 ones. Sometimes the sender's address does not fit in the old format, so this memo says what to put there.

questions: what if icmpv6 source is not translatable
how does a stateless translator pick an icmp source address
why use random ipv4 source from a pool in translation
subtitle: What source address a stateless IPv4/IPv6 translator should use when an ICMPv6 sender has no IPv4 equivalent.

tldr.problem: A stateless IPv4/IPv6 translator can receive ICMPv6 messages from a source that is not an IPv4-translatable address, so there is no obvious IPv4 source address for the translated ICMP message.
tldr.mechanism: The translator uses a single public IPv4 address, or a small pool, as the source, and adds the original IPv6 address through the ICMP extension of RFC 5837. With a pool, it picks the address at random.
tldr.outcome: The ICMP messages cross the translator instead of being dropped, and an enhanced traceroute can still see the real IPv6 sources.

facts.label: Recommended source
facts.value: A single public IPv4 address or a small pool

today: RFC 6791 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2012. It updates RFC 6145, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Gap Left by RFC 6145
sections.content:
Section 5.3 of RFC 6145 notes that the IPv6 addresses in an IPv6 header may not be IPv4-translatable addresses, so no matching IPv4 address exists. It says a stateless way to translate such an address was left for future work.

RFC 6791 provides recommendations for that case. The term "IPv4-translatable IPv6 address" is used as defined in Section 2.2 of RFC 6052. The document updates RFC 6145.
sections.eli5: An earlier rulebook said what to do with most addresses but left one case open. This memo fills in that missing rule.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
Suppose a stateless translator receives an ICMPv6 message, for example Packet Too Big, from a non-IPv4-translatable IPv6 source, and the message is bound for an IPv4-translatable IPv6 address. The translator needs to pick a source address for the ICMP message it generates, and the choice is awkward.

The RFC lists what makes it hard. The address SHOULD NOT cause the ICMP packet to be discarded. It SHOULD NOT come from RFC 1918 or RFC 6598 space, because that space is likely to be subject to unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) filtering.

Translation is meant for places where IPv4 addresses may be scarce, so it is not appropriate to give an IPv4-translatable address to every internal point that might originate ICMPv6 messages.
sections.eli5: The translator has to sign the message with some address. Some addresses get thrown away by guards on the road, and there are not enough good addresses to give every sender its own.

sections.title: Telling Origins Apart
sections.content:
IPv4 recipients should be able to tell different IPv6 origins apart, for example so that a traceroute utility gets some network-level visibility across the translator. That means the translator either needs a pool of IPv4 addresses to map different origins to, or has to carry the IPv6 source information by other means.

The RFC says that, at the time of writing, TRACEROUTE and MTR are the only consumers of translated ICMPv6 messages that care about the ICMPv6 source address.
sections.eli5: Someone tracing a route wants to know which stop each reply came from. If every reply is signed the same way, the stops look the same.

sections.title: The Recommended Approach
sections.content:
The recommended approach is to use a single public IPv4 address, or a small pool of them, as the source of the translated ICMP message. The translator then uses the ICMP extension of RFC 5837 to include the original IPv6 address as an Interface IP Address Sub-Object.

The single address can be the translator's IPv4 interface address or its loopback address. In either the single or pool case, the translator SHOULD implement the RFC 5837 extension, and the ICMP message SHOULD include the sub-object carrying the source IPv6 address of the original ICMPv6 message.
sections.eli5: The translator signs with its own public address and puts the sender's real address in a small note inside the message.

sections.title: Choosing from a Pool
sections.content:
If a pool of public IPv4 addresses is configured, the translator is RECOMMENDED to select the source address from the pool at random. Random selection lowers the chance that two ICMP messages elicited by the same traceroute carry the same source address and so wrongly look like a routing loop.

An enhanced traceroute application that understands the RFC 5837 extension will reveal the IPv6 source addresses that generated the original ICMPv6 messages. The RFC adds that a future ICMP extension could indicate that a packet was translated and that the source address belongs to the translator, not the originating node.
sections.eli5: If the translator has several addresses, it picks one by chance each time, so a traveler does not see the same name twice and think they are going in circles.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document recommends producing IPv4 ICMP messages from IPv6 ICMP messages that would otherwise have been discarded. New considerations are not expected to result from this.

As with a number of ICMP messages, a spoofed source address may cause replies to arrive at hosts that did not expect them, by using the facility of the translator.
sections.eli5: Someone could fake the return address, so a reply might land at a house that never asked for it. That is true of many ICMP messages already.
